And in your evidence yesterday, you gave the following answer at lines -- I asked you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the question as follows on line 14 and the answer that you gave on line 16 is as follows: "Could you first of all give us an approximate date or time when that distribution took place in your presence?" And your answer was: "Yes, all this took place at the beginning of 1991." Is that a correct answer?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- the -- those events took place in the beginning of 1991. When, in the beginning of 1991? Are you able to clarify that further?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the beginning of February and the end of January. We cannot confirm now whether it was the last day in the month of January 1992 or the first day of February 1992, but it's certain that this happened in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice that the question in your testimony yesterday was about 1991 and now you're spontaneously giving further details, you're referring to early 1992. Was it 1991 or was it 1992 or was it -- let's say was it a couple of months before the armed conflict started or was it one year and a half before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking about 15 and 16, then that happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That answers the question and that clarifies the record. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to another area in the examination where I believe there may be an error in the transcript. Yesterday -- and I'm referring, Your Honours, to page 53 of the transcript, specifically line 3 and specifically line 6. For context, Mr. Alajbegovic, this deals with the occasion when Colonel Dragomir Milosevic was present at the barricades and I asked you the question: "Can you inform the Trial Chamber of the relationship between Colonel Dragomir Milosevic and the formations that were under the command of Rajko Kusic?" In your answer, I won't read all of your answer, but I'll read part of it, you said: "And that's what happened. Radomir Milosevic went forward. Rajko Kusic went halfway to meet him. They stopped to talk behind the roadblock and after they emerged, we realised that Rajko Kusic too is under the command of Radomir Milosevic." Is the name Radomir Milosevic the person you were referring to or were you referring to someone else in your answer?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the answer should be -- when it's -- when the answer from yesterday refers to Radomir Milosevic, that should be changed to Dragomir Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's the commander of the barracks in Han Pijesak and later the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, so it's that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a question on cross-examination by Ms. Loukas about the words "ethnic cleansing" and "deportation" and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just so we can assure that we have the correct quotation, the questions -- the specific question that I asked was the terms "deporting" or "expelling." I'll just get my assistant to get the exact page reference for Mr. Harmon's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't need that, Your Honour. I think the witness understood the question and I would just like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Alajbegovic, what happened to the Muslim villages after the -- after May the 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this does not arise from re-examination. My cross-examination was specifically on this topic in relation to the use of specific words and it's quite clear that my cross-examination was focused in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I refer Your Honours to page 5 of the Bosnian statement, the statement he gave to the Bosnian authorities, and while we are talking about words, I'm talking about what happened and it is consistent with the words that were testified to by this witness. There's no number and lines in this but I'm referring to the middle of the page, who he has discussed ultimatums and ultimatums to turn in weapons, and if Your Honours turn to page 5 - paragraph 6, actually, but it's on page 5, in the middle of the page, there is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 5, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is paragraph 6 but it's page 5 and will you see where he describes what happened when there was no compliance with the ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've looked at that paragraph myself and it's quite clear what my questions in cross-examination were about to a police officer of 30 years who knows how to give specific evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you're now repeating -- if you give me an opportunity to read exactly ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Ms. Loukas did not pay any attention to what happened but exclusively dealt with the words used during the negotiations and the ultimatums which is a chapter which is not the same as what actually happened so therefore, the later events are in evidence as part of the Bosnian statement. So therefore, that's a separate chapter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alajbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you, Mr. Alajbegovic, unless Ms. Loukas, the questions put by Mr. Harmon would raise any need.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Mr. Harmon's re-examination is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took that more or less from the character of his questions. Yes. Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. I'm talking about the period preceding the events -- on the eve of these unfortunate events. I'm talking about that period, and I would like to understand how the institutions worked, the institutions you belonged to. Therefore, I would like you to try to use your imagination. You have witnessed a crime, an ordinary crime, let's assume that; do you understand what I mean? You see that this crime has been committed and I suppose in this situation, you draw up a report even if you do not arrest the perpetrator of the crime. Once this report has been drafted, whom do you send it to? You don't keep all these notes to yourself.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were reports because the sequence of events was that the legal organs of authority of the Rogatica municipality since the war conflicts broke out were active at a war location which was dislocated from ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not talking about the events that took place during the war. I'm not talking about that. I'm talking about the events of everyday life. You are a police officer. You find out that a crime or crimes have been committed, crimes that I would call ordinary, crimes that have nothing to do with any conflict whatsoever. What is the procedure that you follow in this case? From the time when you find out that a crime has been committed, what do you do with your notes, with your reports? Whom do you send them to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and my associates, the people -- the operative officers in the police force on the territory of the Rogatica municipality, once we arrive at the police station, we would jointly compile, and I set out the main concept or said what happened and then the typists would do their part of the job, we would compile the document, and the documents would be sent to the chief of the police station to sign, and then he would assess -- it would be up to him to assess whether to send it forward up the ladder to the SUP or to telephone them, because some information was communicated by telephone. Now, as far as criminal responsibility is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you send that to the SUP. You said that the SUP was the secretary to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republican.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the republic.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republican Secretariat of Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And one copy of the document would remain in our archives, in the documents of our office, the office I was in at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, at some point, the prosecutor or the judges had to be seized of these reports at some point, so who would transmit, who would submit these reports to the prosecutor or to the judges?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the department of our crime police, our crime police department who maintained contact with the Prosecutor who was then active in the Rogatica area. Now, in view of the fact that he was a Serb by ethnicity, he didn't do much, he didn't mind much about things like that, and considered them -- the evidence that we provided to be material that wasn't serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second question: Yesterday, you told us that when you found out the facts that you mentioned when you were a witness, for example, of the unloading of weapons from military trucks, when you said that pictures were taken, pictures of crates of ammunition that had been unloaded, you gave an answer to one of my questions and you said that you drew up a report and that you sent that report to the SUP. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What sort of reaction did you expect from the Secretariat of the Interior Ministry from the SUP, what sort of reaction did you expect from them, what response?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected a positive reaction and permission to take more concrete steps on the ground to disarm the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so you never received these instructions.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. There was no feedback information. Everything stopped there. It was just an oral agreement that we shouldn't complicate matters and that we should stop the proceedings, and then once the circumstances were right, certain steps might be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. You told us that you were in command of several dozens of people, you were the superior of a number of policemen. You mentioned about 100 policemen, if I remember properly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The formation numbered 210 police employees, it was based on a multi-ethnic principle, a full complement based on multi-ethnicity from the ranks of Serbs and Muslims alike. The ratio was 60 to 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 60 per cent of what?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims. 60 per cent Muslims and 40 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What prevented you from sending your men to intervene following these events, these facts? When you were a witness to the unloading of weapons of -- and when you saw that these weapons were distributed to members of the civilian population, what prevented you from taking steps, together with your men?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is a very simple one: In all these operations, the commander took part and with respect to war plans and whatever, it was Mr. Mladen Vasiljevic, which means that I couldn't take any steps bypassing him. I informed the chief of the police station, as I have already told you; that's all I could do. And then the process went on that way. I was told not to take any measures because it would complicate the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, what would have happened if you had played the role, the part that had been defined for you by your institution? You were a representative of the state, you had an authority as a police officer. What would have happened if you had made use of that power, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My powers went along the lines of applying the provisions that were in force of the Criminal Code; however, in view of the fact that the situation was a complicated one on the ground and as the superiors assessed the situation and their conclusion was that we shouldn't cause problems or conflicts, let time tell and put it off. Because there were attacks that were being planned against the Muslim population in Rogatica. So that was the point. That's why the legal provisions were not applied by the legal organs of power and authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you say that you did not agree with that way of going about things?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but my position could do nothing to change matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my very last question: What was your duty? According to your duty, what were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty was to provide information through the police stations in the field from the local communes to deal with all the -- with the problem in hand, to assess it, to see the security situation and how far both ethnic groups were threatened, to assess the activities of the police, and to present all that material and report to the head of the police station. According to the hierarchy, the chain of command going upwards, he would inform the competent ministry or Secretariat of the -- of Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got two questions to you as well, one in -- as a follow-up from the questions put to you by Judge Hanoteau. Was your position such that you had to obey orders from your superiors or could you proceed on your own authority in these sensitive matters of arming civilians?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't do anything independently, but through the method of information, they asked me my opinion and these were assessed -- this was assessed by my superiors, the more responsible people in the Rogatica area and the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the higher instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was your direct superior in the Rogatica area?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already taken note of that but I'll repeat it again. The head of the police station was Mr. Ismet Osmanovic who, at that time, was the acting president of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he explicitly instruct you not to further proceed and not to further investigate the distribution of arms?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't explicit in the context but he always said that we should wait to see how matters developed, all with the aim of putting off a conflict, and the feedback information that we received -- that reached me was that he, either in written form or oral form, did inform the competent authorities in the Ministry for the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that usual in relation to such sensitive issues, that instructions or orders were rather implicit than explicit? Do you understand what I mean? Just to give you an example, I can say: "I instruct you not to investigate this." Or as a superior, I could say, "I think it would be wise that no further investigations take place in this respect," which is not an explicit order. But what was the tone, I would say, in those sensitive areas? Was this uncommon that there was no explicit order or was that common?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that point in time, for us, it was not definite. The Serb people didn't lack weapons because the Yugoslav People's Army had too many weapons, a surplus of weapons, and if he were to issue orders that we should investigate, then this might lead to direct conflict, which was not the aim nor the policy pursued by the Democratic Action Party that he led, all in the aim of keeping the peace and coexistence in the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it's not a direct answer to my question, I would like to move to another subject. Yesterday, you told us about the facts that supported your impression that Dragomir Milosevic had command over Mr. Kusic and his formation. You told us that Mr. Milosevic insisted on separation effected through blockades and that this became effective once Mr. Kusic and his formation arrived, and that's -- that made you conclude that Mr. Milosevic had command over Kusic and his formation. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We drew the conclusion that at that point in time, through the Kusic/Milosevic talks at the barricades and Kusic listening to the orders to disband the blockade, which didn't mean a great deal at that time because there was other blockades towards the enclave of the Zepa local commune, that Kusic was directly under the command of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, you give further information now, but since you yesterday very much insisted that at the arrival of the Kusic formation, the wishes of Mr. Milosevic -- well, were -- became effective through these formations, I would like to put to you that if one assumes that Mr. Milosevic had similar wishes as Mr. Kusic would have, then would it not be true that upon the arrival of the Kusic formation, that even if there would have been no command relationship between Milosevic and Kusic, that the Kusic formations could have created a same result, could have created a same effect if Kusic wanted the same as Milosevic wanted, not because he was ordered to do what Milosevic wanted, but because he wanted it himself? I'm just putting this because you said, "Upon arrival, this is what happened; therefore, that was a command relationship between Milosevic and Kusic." I'm now creating a picture in which two persons not linked in a command relationship wished to do the same and therefore the factual situation might be exactly the same as you described but now without a command relationship between Milosevic and Kusic. That was a very long question. Could you comment on this possibility?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best in providing an answer and showing you the sequence of events. We're talking about the 25th of March. Milosevic had more intelligence information about upcoming operations of Serb military and paramilitary forces and the forces of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army for attacks on Sarajevo, and most probably he wanted to put off negotiations in April for the Rogatica area because the number of men, the forces, and later on we saw that was true, that they would be transferred to the Sarajevo battleground, theatre of operation. So that was some -- it appeared as if Kusic, at that point in time, was not hierarchically linked up, was not under the command of General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say was not hierarchically linked but nevertheless, your testimony yesterday was that he had -- or he exercised command of the Kusic formation. You say if it's not in a hierarchy, what, then, made Milosevic be in the position of commanding Kusic and his formation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an authority as a military superior and the man -- the top man for the Romanija Corps coming -- that Rogatica came under, and Kusic was aware of that. Now, whether he was hierarchically subordinate on the basis of documents, I don't know, but one gained the impression that he was, and this is what became apparent on the spot at the barricade, because it was from this barricade that officially, to his commander, the deputy to Milosevic, Dzambasovic, Kusic criticised him. He said, "What are you waiting for? Go and line up the Muslim army." Several days later, from Sarajevo by phone, he phoned me, the head of the police station, Mr. Dzambasovic called me up personally, informing us that he was on holiday at that point in time, and that was a whole scenario. It meant that the role ceased at that point in time of the Muslim representative in the units of the army as Milosevic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Any need for further questions in relation to the questions put by the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no questions arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same for you, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, same for me, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Alajbegovic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. We'd like to thank you for having come far away to The Hague and having answered all questions, both questions of the parties and of the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Alajbegovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibits, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P565 has been reserved for the witness statement compiled on 10 May 1996 before the investigating judge of the high court in Sarajevo, the redacted version to be tendered by the Prosecution to the Registry. Exhibit P566 has been reserved for ICTY witness statement dated 26 January 1999, the corrected version to be tendered to -- by the Prosecution to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same is true for the translations, because there was the bottleneck, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the bottleneck applies only to P566. The changes that were made in the Bosnian statement were the changes that in paragraph 1 of the date, as I recall, changed from 1974 to 1979, and in the last paragraph there was a date, that number changed from 14 to 15, so I think we are prepared to tender those particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 566, yes, with the two dates, the two numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Changed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Those will be handed in to the registrar after the first -- after the next break, Your Honour, but we're prepared to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll receive that soon but -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

P572, colour map and graph of the ethnic composition of Rogatica annotated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to make a suggestion to the parties, and that is the following: Ms. Loukas, you have expressed your objections against the ICTY statement, at least certain parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, Mr. Harmon, you are redacting in view of the changes made by the witness, that statement, could you try to agree on whether there should be any deletions. I mean, Ms. Loukas dealt with certain parts. Of course, some of the bits of the testimony of the witness has clarified issues or -- and sometimes it's better to leave the original text in it because reference is made to that; on the other hand, we also have parts where a deletion would not harm at all because the witness fully testified on that issue in viva voce testimony, and then I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can imagine that if that is not exactly the same as what we find on paper, that Ms. Loukas would rather concentrate on the viva voce testimony. Would there be a possibility that the parties agree whether any, apart from the changes necessary on the basis of the testimony of the witness, whether any smaller parts could be taken out such as to meet your concerns about the content, whether the parties could agree on that so that we have a final version which does not need any further amending?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to enter into discussions with Mr. Harmon on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am too, Your Honour. On the other hand, often times there is reference to the paragraph and what's in certain paragraphs, and I think that would confuse the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it should be done with common sense, I would say, of course. Sometimes it's not just ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure that both Mr. Harmon and I can approach the matter with some common sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am fully confident as well. So any further objections to the exhibits then, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, on the part of the Defence, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means apart from P566, all the other exhibits are admitted into evidence and the Chamber will later decide on the amended version of P566. Then is the -- the next witness to be called for the Prosecution arrives for cross-examination only and protective measures are in place, which are, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the protective measures, protective measures, closed session, and as a consequence of a decision taken by another Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I wonder what would be a wise thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For many reasons, and I apologise to you, Mr. Hannis, the Chamber would prefer to have an early break, so to have a 20-minutes break now because some technical matters have to be dealt with which is better done in the absence of the Chamber, and we would then restart at 12.25 and then continue until a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there's just one matter I should place on the record at this point very quickly, and that is that during my conference with Mr. Krajisnik yesterday, it became apparent that he hadn't been informed that the name of the next witness, the witness we're about to deal with now, and I won't mention the name because of the protective measures, so I gave Mr. Krajisnik the material in B/C/S that I had in my possession in relation to this witness so that he could look at it overnight. I think there was some changes between the weeks, between last week and this week, and apparently the information that I thought had been conveyed to Mr. Krajisnik had not been conveyed to him in terms of the identity of the next witness, because there were some last-minute changes about the order and what have you. In any event, I have provided that information to Mr. Krajisnik in the conference that we had yesterday, so subsequent to Mr. Hannis dealing with the 92 bis aspects, I will need an opportunity for a further short conference with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this, then, not be the best -- the next 20 minutes, or you would need more time?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would need more than 20 minutes, that's why I mention it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My computer might need 30 minutes, so if that would do, Ms. Loukas, but of course, it's -- of course changes have been made but the next witness is on the list already for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but Your Honour is quite aware of the changes.
